output.query: SOD1 A4V ALS mutation prognosis survival management

results.finding: The A4V variant accounts for approximately 50% of SOD1-related motor neuron disease cases in North America. Median survival from symptom onset is 11.6 months (range 6 months to 4 years). Predominantly LMN presentation initially. Rapid respiratory failure is the principal cause of death.
results.title: SOD1 A4V: aggressive familial motor neuron disease variant

results.finding: Tofersen (Qalsody) received FDA approval in April 2023 for adults with ALS associated with a mutation in SOD1. Administered as an intrathecal injection every 4 weeks. Reduces SOD1 protein levels in CSF and plasma. Phase 3 trials demonstrated reduction in neurofilament light chain accumulation; evidence for functional benefit continues to accumulate.
results.title: SOD1 antisense oligonucleotide therapy (tofersen)

output.formulary_status: FDA approved for SOD1-mediated motor neuron disease (Qalsody). Covered with diagnosis confirmation and genetic testing.
interactions: Riluzole: no pharmacokinetic interaction with intrathecal tofersen. Can coadminister both.

warnings: Tofersen intrathecal: lumbar puncture every 4 weeks required. Risks include post-procedural headache, meningitis. Lumbar access required.
Neuroinflammation (pleocytosis, elevated protein) can occur — monitor CSF at each administration

output.query: SOD1 A4V ALS genetic counseling family members predictive testing

results.finding: SOD1-related motor neuron disease follows autosomal dominant inheritance with approximately 80-90% penetrance by age 80. Each first-degree relative of an affected individual has a 50% risk of inheriting the pathogenic variant. Predictive genetic testing is available for at-risk relatives and should be offered with appropriate genetic counseling. Pre-symptomatic antisense oligonucleotide therapy in confirmed presymptomatic carriers is under clinical investigation.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not commit the patient to cervical spine surgery on the basis of incidental spondylotic changes when EMG findings extend beyond the cervical cord.
Do not start chronic immunosuppression (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) for ALS — there is no benefit and treatment delays correct diagnosis.
Do not defer respiratory assessment in a symptomatic patient — even mild FVC reduction warrants close monitoring and NIV planning.
Do not dismiss bulbar or progressive symptoms as functional / psychiatric without a complete neurological workup.
required_recommendations: Perform EMG/NCS sampling the bulbar region plus ≥2 spinal regions to document lower-motor-neuron involvement and exclude conduction block.
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural mimics (cervical myelopathy, demyelinating disease, brainstem tumor).
Order a mimic-exclusion lab panel (CK, B12, TSH, HIV, RPR, SPEP, anti-GM1 IgM, androgen receptor CAG repeat in males).
Measure baseline respiratory function (FVC, MIP/MEP, SNIP) to inform NIV timing.
Apply Awaji-Shima 2008 / Gold Coast 2020 criteria to confirm the diagnosis.
Initiate riluzole 50 mg twice daily after baseline LFTs unless contraindicated; arrange monthly LFT monitoring for the first 3 months.
Refer to a multidisciplinary ALS clinic for SLP, dietetics, respiratory, and social-work input.
Order an ALS-focused genetic panel (C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS, TBK1) and arrange genetic counseling.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Diagnosis requires evidence of both upper-motor-neuron involvement (hyperreflexia, Babinski, Hoffman, brisk jaw jerk, spasticity) and lower-motor-neuron involvement (atrophy, fasciculations, EMG denervation) with progressive spread, while excluding mimics — Awaji 2008 / Gold Coast 2020.

EMG in bulbar plus ≥2 spinal regions documenting fibrillations, positive sharp waves, complex fasciculation potentials, and large-amplitude long-duration polyphasic MUPs with reduced recruitment satisfies the electrodiagnostic criterion.
Normal sensory NCS and absence of conduction block are pivotal: they exclude common mimics including multifocal motor neuropathy, CIDP, and Kennedy disease.
Mild-to-moderate CK elevation (2–5× ULN) is consistent with ALS and does not itself indicate a primary myopathy.
Cervical spondylotic changes on MRI are common incidental findings in the at-risk age group; bulbar findings or multi-region EMG denervation cannot be attributed to cervical disease.
Baseline FVC, MIP/MEP, and SNIP/NIF inform NIV timing — NIV initiation at FVC <50% predicted or SNIP <40 cmH₂O prolongs survival and improves quality of life.
Young-onset or family history justifies genetic testing — C9orf72 is the most common cause and has implications for FTD risk and family counseling; SOD1 carriers may be eligible for tofersen.

July 2026 review applied end to end: EMG/NCS is the required ALS-specific test; brain and cord MRI and targeted labs exclude mimics; respiratory function is a recommended safety baseline; genetics is separately offered after counselling; CSF is absent except in five atypical mimic work-ups.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. C is a 45-year-old retired professional swimmer who presents with a 6-month history of widespread muscle fasciculations and subtle weakness. He noticed fasciculations first in his calves 8 months ago and they have spread to his thighs and bilateral arms. He recently learned that his paternal uncle died of ALS at age 52, which has caused significant anxiety.

He reports mild weakness compared to his prior athletic baseline — he can no longer swim his usual training distances without unusual fatigue and has reduced performance in gym workouts. He notes apparent reduction in bilateral calf bulk. He has no swallowing, speech, or sensory symptoms.

Several features complicate interpretation: his former elite athletic status gives him a high baseline strength and reflex level, so a 'normal' standard examination may represent significant loss from his personal baseline; the bilateral calf muscle loss is ambiguous, potentially reflecting detraining since retiring 2 years ago or denervation atrophy; and the widespread fasciculations occur in someone with a history of intense physical training, in whom fasciculations are common. His paternal uncle died of ALS at age 52. On current examination, reflexes are brisk (3+) compared with a prior 2+, an interval increase, with no clear upper motor neuron signs yet.

neurological_exam.additional: Former elite swimmer; baseline muscle mass and reflex levels may differ from non-athlete norms. Calf atrophy may represent detraining vs true denervation.

neurological_exam.motor: Fasciculations visible in bilateral thighs, calves, and both arms at rest. Muscle bulk appears reduced bilateral calves vs expected for former athlete. Strength tests: appears near-normal 4+/5 to 5-/5 throughout — submaximal effort difficult to exclude given anxiety. No clear focal weakness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally (previously documented 2+ by PCP). Brachioradialis 3+. Knee jerks 3+ (previously 2+). No Hoffman. No Babinski — plantar responses flexor.
